body.text: When I visited jeepney drivers protesting rising oil prices, one of them told me how his family had lost their home and could no longer afford rent. They now sleep in their jeepney. Their story is heartbreaking, but hardly isolated. I have met elementary schoolchildren who miss classes because their families can’t afford fares. College students leave classes early to reach their side jobs because rising electricity bills mean they must now contribute to their families’ expenses. These are the choices rising energy costs force on Filipino families today.

After the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, retail gasoline prices in Metro Manila skyrocketed by 60 percent and diesel by 70 percent, exposing our vulnerability to global shocks and forcing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a national energy emergency in March 2026. Our power bills tell the same story today. The Philippines routinely posts ASEAN’s highest average electricity rates, peaking at 12.43 Philippine pesos per kilowatt-hour in June. Imported coal and gas make up more than 70 percent of our power mix, and we import more than 90 percent of our oil. Families are at the mercy of volatile global prices.

The energy crisis was a wake-up call for the region, and Southeast Asia is ready to transition. Since the war, the region’s six major economies have announced four times as many long-term renewable energy policies as fossil fuel ones. The Philippines alone fast-tracked 1,471 MW of green energy and storage. Our rooftop solar capacity has nearly doubled since early 2025.

This is the transition Japan’s regional framework was supposed to support. When Japan launched the Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) in 2023, it presented the platform as a way to pursue decarbonization alongside economic growth and energy security.

The record says otherwise. Research found that of AZEC’s 329 initiatives, renewable generation accounted for a meager 14-22 percent. Grid infrastructure and energy storage received a negligible 2-5 percent. Meanwhile, projects designed to keep fossil-fuel thermal plants running via ammonia co-firing, hydrogen blending, or carbon capture made up 13-20 percent.

A separate analysis found that 35 percent of the AZEC agreements signed in 2023 and 2024 lack any public documentation, and of the projects that could be traced, only 18 percent had transitioned into development or operation. The same analysis also found that some of the projects “may be connected to a credit and offset program for Japanese companies to meet their own targets under Japan’s emissions trading system.”

AZEC’s own policy report betrays its climate mandate, insisting that coal should be maintained as a regional backstop, championing “clean coal” technologies for aging infrastructure, and positioning liquefied natural gas as a permanent cornerstone fuel.

But in the wake of this year’s Hormuz crisis, Japan seemingly stopped presenting AZEC as an emissions reduction initiative and returned to its fossil fuel agenda. In April, it convened an AZEC leaders’ meeting launched its Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia, or POWERR Asia, a $10 billion financial package focused heavily on alternative crude procurement and immediate oil stockpiling.

It is not a lifeline for countries facing fuel shortages. For the Philippines, its main output so far is a stockpile feasibility study, with physical stocks not scheduled until early 2028 – far too late to solve our immediate energy anxieties.

The Japanese government noted that the financial support under POWERR serves companies facing supply chain vulnerabilities regarding imports to Japan. It can even directly finance resource imports by Japanese corporations themselves through a public finance framework that supports supply chains for energy and critical materials. Japan’s own ambassador for AZEC framed these new emergency responses to address immediate fuel shortages and maintain supply chains across Asia. Behind the lofty language of regional solidarity lies a motive: protecting Japan’s supply chains, regardless of what Southeast Asia actually needs.
Japan has every right to defend its own trade networks. But it has no right to dress up its domestic fossil fuel strategy as a regional partnership for decarbonization and energy security.

This November, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae will co-chair the fourth AZEC Leaders’ Summit with Marcos, and will almost certainly present it as a moment to prioritize Southeast Asia’s energy security and economic interests. As host, the Philippines must be the first to scrutinize what AZEC and POWERR Asia have delivered and for whom.

As lawmakers, we have a responsibility to scrutinize agreements made in our people’s name: who finances these projects, who profits from them, and who ultimately shoulders the costs. Marcos must not allow the Philippines to become another market for fossil fuel infrastructure that will keep future generations paying for today’s decisions.

Southeast Asia does not lack political will or resources. We lack grid infrastructure, modern storage capacity, and cheap capital to distribute this power. Japanese capital could fund that infrastructure and unlock clean, affordable energy for millions of households. Instead, Japan is using its diplomatic weight to lock the region into fossil fuel dependency.

Southeast Asia needs a structural escape from volatile energy imports, not a repackaging of the exact same fossil fuel trap. Japan cannot expect us to foot the bill or act as its regional oil storage locker. Japan must use its power, influence, and finance to build a genuine exit from fossil fuels with us. The transition must also change who owns and controls our energy. We need community-based solar, mini-hydro, and other small-scale renewable systems owned by the people. Japan could support local clean technology manufacturing and develop Filipino technical capacity instead of adding fossil fuel debt to our burden.

Energy is a right. When our leaders meet in Manila, they should remember the families who can no longer afford to keep a roof over their heads or send their children to school. As host, the Philippines must make it clear what path we need Japan to take.
